questions.question: Why should Consultative Prompting be taught as a workflow instead of only as tool awareness?
options: Because teams need shared signals, controls, and decision rules they can apply to real work
Because a professional-looking workshop agenda is proof the prompt improved the consulting work
Because asking the model for more text is the reliable way to sharpen a weak hypothesis
Because client context only matters once the recommendation has already been drafted
questions.explanation: The lesson is built around reusable operating artifacts — shared signals, controls, and decision rules — not the idea that a polished agenda proves better consulting, that more generated text sharpens a hypothesis, or that client context can wait until after the recommendation.

questions.question: In the lesson's opening example, what was missing from the professional-looking workshop agenda the assistant drafted?
options: Stakeholder tension, decision criteria, risks, and the specific client context the work depended on
A source-grounded reading list, which the consultant had planned to attach to the agenda later
A summary of the six consulting moves: clarify, diagnose, structure, challenge, synthesize, recommend
An audience-fit rewrite for the steering committee, which was scheduled for the following week
questions.explanation: The lesson's opening example is an agenda that reads professionally but reflects none of the stakeholder tension, decision criteria, risks, or client context — the prompt produced output without improving the consulting work. A missing reading list, a list of consulting moves, or an audience rewrite are not what the example turns on.

questions.question: What does the Python artifact produce for Consultative Prompting?
options: A ranked plan with category, score, priority, controls, and rationale
A finished workshop agenda that needs no further consultant review at all
A single quality score for a prompt, with no rationale attached
A transcript of the client meeting that the prompt prepared for
questions.explanation: The lesson's Python artifact outputs a ranked plan — category, score, priority, controls, and rationale — not a review-free workshop agenda, a bare prompt-quality score, or a meeting transcript.

questions.question: Which control belongs to the lesson design?
options: Skipping the counterargument step because the agenda already reads as balanced and professional
An assumption check, so the prompt forces the model to reveal what it took for granted
Dropping source grounding once the model's answer matches the consultant's own hypothesis
Writing every prompt for the same audience so the wording stays consistent across clients
questions.explanation: The lesson's controls include an assumption check that makes the model reveal what it took for granted — the opposite of skipping the counterargument, dropping source grounding when the answer is agreeable, or ignoring audience fit.

questions.question: When should a scenario become a launch-gate discussion rather than a casual awareness exercise?
options: Only when the client happens to be an external customer rather than an internal team
When impact, uncertainty, and matched risk signals such as stakeholder tension are all high
Only when the prompt pack is being used for a proposal rather than a regular meeting
Never — a generic AI-drafted agenda can always be fixed in the room during the workshop — and applies unchanged even when the lesson's stated preconditions fail
questions.explanation: High-impact, uncertain, tension-heavy consulting situations need a launch gate regardless of whether the client is external, which document the prompt pack feeds, or whether the facilitator expects to fix things live.

questions.question: What is the main purpose of the output template?
options: To create a reusable prompt pack that teams can keep applying after the course ends
To formally replace the consultant's own judgment about the client recommendation, with no need to inspect intermediate results or test edge cases
To keep the weakest assumptions in a hypothesis away from the steering committee
To automatically generate completion certificates once the workshop has finished
questions.explanation: The output template is a consultative prompt pack for discovery, synthesis, and recommendation work that teams keep applying after the course — not a substitute for the consultant's judgment, a way to hide weak assumptions from steering, or an automatic certificate generator.
